notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 71. I've included only what the pages I read actually say. Each point ends with its URL.

**Background (whole psalm)**
- **Who wrote it?** Guzik notes that many commentators think it is David's prayer during Absalom's rebellion. Because the psalm has no title, he treats it as anonymous. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the mention of old age fits Adonijah's rebellion better than Absalom's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/71.htm
- In Spurgeon's *Treasury*, William Binnie agrees with Calvin and the older writers that David wrote it in his old age. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- Spurgeon calls the whole psalm "struggling, but unstaggering, faith." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- **Borrowed language:** Guzik lists echoes of Psalms 31, 22, 70 and 35 and of Exodus 15. He suggests the writer had soaked himself in Scripture for a lifetime. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- **Catholic/patristic:** Augustine (Psalm 70 in his numbering) works from a title that mentions the sons of Jonadab and the first captives. He reads the psalm as a song of God's delivering grace, Christ freeing us from the captivity that came through Adam. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801071.htm

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the psalm opens by looking to God rather than describing the trouble. The writer trusts that this trust will be vindicated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- The Cambridge Bible translates "have taken refuge." The prayer is that he will never be disgraced by finding his trust was in vain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-1.htm
- Matthew Henry: God never disappoints a hope he himself has raised. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_071.cfm

**v. 2**
- Spurgeon reads "in your righteousness" as "be true to your word." It is right for God to keep his promises to those who trust him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- A note in the *Treasury* says the appeal is to God's righteousness, not his own. The writer pleads no merit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- NET note: the Hebrew is "in your vindication." Psalm 31:1 leaves out "and deliver me." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=71
- Bob Utley (bible.org): "incline your ear" is a human picture of God, used to ask him to hear. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-71

**v. 3**
- Matthew Henry: "give the command to save me" means God has promised it. God's promises are so effective that they work like commands, as in "Let there be light." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_071.cfm
- Ellicott: the second "rock" should be read as "cliff." The Hebrew word differs from the one used earlier. https://biblehub.com/psalms/71-3.htm
- NET: the picture is of a rocky, hard-to-reach summit that protects from enemies. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=71
- Augustine: he is only safe if God is his "walled place." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801071.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: there seems to be one particular wicked, cruel man holding the psalmist in his grip. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- The Pulpit Commentary says David typically singles out one enemy among many. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/71.htm
- Spurgeon: the enemies are God's enemies too, so God will rescue his own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-1.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: God is not only the one he hopes in; God is his hope. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- Augustine reads "from my youth" as starting when he began to hope in God, that is, at conversion. Before that, God protected him without his knowing it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801071.htm

**v. 6**
- Calvin (quoted in the *Treasury*): David praises God's goodness from before he was born. We undervalue the miracle of birth only because it is so familiar. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- Matthew Henry: the God who helped us from birth should be our hope from youth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/71.htm
- Barnes: since God has kept him from his earliest years, he has reason to ask God to keep him into old age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-71.html

**v. 7 ("portent")**
Commentators disagree on what this word means:
- Ellicott: a *monster*, someone people point at and avoid, not a miracle of rescue. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-71.html
- Barnes: God's dealings with him were so unusual that they drew attention the way miracles do. He most likely means many afflictions and many rescues. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-71.html
- Constable: onlookers took what was happening to him as an omen that God was abandoning the righteous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-71.html
- Matthew Henry gives two options: people are watching to see how it ends, or they shun him as a monster. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_071.cfm
- Guzik cites Kidner: the words "but you" turn his attention away from himself and his enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/

**v. 8**
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik): God's bread is always in our mouths, so his praise should be too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/

**v. 9**
- Spurgeon: old age takes away strength but does not lower us in God's favour. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- Guzik: strength can also fail spiritually. He gives David, Solomon and Asa as people who declined later in life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- Barnes: the best thing to lay up for old age is God's favour, sought in youth. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/psalms-71.html
- **Applied to Christ:** a writer in the *Treasury* says Christ uses vv. 9 and 18 in sympathy with his people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm

**vv. 10–11**
- Spurgeon: the enemies claimed God would forsake him, so he prays all the harder that God's faithfulness will prove them liars. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- Guzik links the taunt "God has forsaken him" to the mocking of Jesus at the cross (Luke 23). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- Augustine reads it as Christ being seized after enemies said in their hearts that God had forsaken him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801071.htm
- Utley: the Hebrew tense of "has forsaken" suggests they think his rejection is permanent. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-71

**v. 12**
- Guzik: this echoes Psalm 22:11 and Psalm 70:1. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- Spurgeon notes the move from "O God" to "O my God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/

**v. 13 (prayer against enemies)**
- Guzik: he wants the enemies discredited, not just defeated. Adam Clarke (Methodist) took the "let them" lines as predictions rather than wishes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- Kidner (cited by Guzik): "vindication, not vindictiveness." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-71.cfm
- The *Treasury* observes that he does not ask God to harm them, only that they be confounded and shamed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- The Biblical Illustrator, by contrast, says he calls for judgment "in the spirit of the Old Testament rather than of the New." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-71.html

**v. 14**
- Guzik sees this as the turning point, from desperation to determination. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- Pulpit: the Hebrew literally means "I will add to all your praise," and "as for me" marks a turn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-14.htm
- Spurgeon: when he cannot enjoy what he has, he looks forward to what will be his. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Spurgeon: creatures have number and limit, but God's grace has neither, so the theme never runs out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- Wesley (Methodist): "the numbers" means the many rescues and mercies God has given him. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/71.htm
- Utley gives two possible meanings: God's acts are too many to count, or too great to understand. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-71

**v. 16: the main place where traditions differ**
The question is what "your righteousness, yours alone" means.
- **Baptist (Gill):** the imputed righteousness of Christ. Justification is not partly by Christ's righteousness and partly by ours, but by his alone, through faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/71-16.html
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** man's righteousness is "filthy rags." He sets this against "the power of sacraments, and the infallibility of pontiffs." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps071.php
- **Reformed (Calvin):** David keeps his mind fixed on God's righteousness alone in order to persevere. Hopes from other quarters lead to falling away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/71-16.html
- **Methodist (Wesley):** the righteousness is God's "faithfulness in making good all thy promises," and he mentions it to comfort himself by remembering it. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/71.htm
- **Methodist (Clarke):** God's acts of mercy and goodness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/71-16.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** he credits his deliverance to God's faithfulness and truth, not to any strength or righteousness of his own. It also notes the Revised Version's "I will come with the mighty acts." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-71.html
- **Catholic/patristic (Augustine):** he refuses to boast in his own strength or in "the letter." He says God taught him that grace comes *gratis* (freely), with no merit of his own coming first. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801071.htm
- On "I will go," Musculus (in the *Treasury*) says it means going into battle. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm

**v. 17**
- Benson: God taught him through his parents, the Word and the Spirit, and his own experience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-17.htm
- Spurgeon: he never left his first teacher, and calls for a "sacred conservatism." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-17.htm
- Augustine: since his conversion he has learned that no merit of his came first. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801071.htm

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: he asks to be kept not for his own sake but to impress God's might on the rising generation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-18.htm
- NET: the Hebrew says "your arm," a human picture for God's strength. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=71
- Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: old age is either pitiful or beautiful, depending on its witness to the young. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- The *Treasury* warns that falling away in old age is a fearful thing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: "to the height," meaning the heavens. It echoes Exodus 15:11. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/71-19.html
- Gill takes it as Christ's righteousness accepted in heaven. Wesley simply glosses it "most eminent." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/71-19.html
- Utley: "who is like you?" asserts that the LORD is unique. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-71

**v. 20**
- **Text question:** the written Hebrew says "us," while the marginal reading says "me." Ellicott thinks "us" shows the psalm was a hymn for the congregation. Barnes prefers "us." Pulpit thinks he is joining his people to himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-20.htm
- Cambridge: "depths of the earth" can mean the underground waters or the place of the dead (Sheol). Pulpit takes it as a picture of extreme misery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-20.htm
- Matthew Henry: God "showed" him troubles, as a father shows a child the rod. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_071.cfm
- **Christ and resurrection:** the *Treasury* reports that Jerome applied the verse to Christ, since David never died and rose again. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm
- Chuck Smith reads it as David's confidence in resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/71-19.html
- The Bible Hub study notes call the verse "suggestive of resurrection." https://biblehub.com/psalms/71.htm
- NET: the verbs can be read as a prayer or as a statement of confidence. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=71

**v. 21**
- NET: the verb form is a wish or prayer. Asking for "greatness" is not a self-serving request; it asks God to vindicate him over those humiliating him. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=71
- Guzik, by contrast, calls it a confident declaration rather than a prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-71/
- Cambridge: elsewhere the word "greatness" is normally used of God. The Greek translation reads "thy righteousness." He may be sharing in the restored nation's honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-21.htm
- Gill reads it as both outward greatness (the revolt crushed) and spiritual greatness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/71-21.htm

**v. 22**
- Pulpit: harp and lyre together suggest public praise in the sanctuary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/71.htm
- Matthew Henry: it is God's honour to be holy, and his people's honour that he is the Holy One *of Israel*. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_071.cfm
- Utley: "Holy One of Israel" is a covenant title used often in Isaiah. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21570

**v. 23**
- NET: "which you have redeemed" works as a future perfect. By then God will have rescued him. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=71
- Matthew Henry: we do not make melody to God unless we sing with the heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_071.cfm
- The *Treasury* traces the word "great" through vv. 19–23. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps071.cfm

**v. 24**
- Pulpit: music can only happen now and then, but the tongue can talk of God all the time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/71.htm
- Barnes: "talk" can mean meditating aloud, the overflow of a full heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-71.html
- Constable: he speaks of the enemies' shame as already done, to express confidence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-71.html
- Spurgeon makes his theme God's "way of justifying sinners." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps071.php

**What I couldn't find:** I found no Lutheran, Orthodox, Anglican or Pentecostal-specific comment on this psalm. Guzik (enduringword) writes in a broadly evangelical way and takes no distinctly Pentecostal line here. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on Psalm 71, so I've left those out.
